grammar.title: Reported speech
grammar.explanation_pt:
Para relatar o que alguém disse, usamos **say** e **tell** e geralmente **voltamos um tempo** no passado (backshift):

**Say x tell:**
- **say** (something) (**to someone**): "She **said** (that) she was busy." / "She **said to me** that..."
- **tell + pessoa** (sempre com objeto!): "She **told me** (that) she was busy." (❌ "She said me" / ❌ "She told that...")

**Backshift (quando o verbo introdutório está no passado):**
- present simple → past simple: "I **work** here." → She said she **worked** there.
- present continuous → past continuous: "I'**m leaving**." → He said he **was leaving**.
- present perfect / past simple → past perfect: "I'**ve finished**." / "I **finished**." → She said she **had finished**.
- will → would: "I'**ll help**." → He said he **would help**.
- can → could: "I **can** come." → She said she **could** come.
- must → had to: "You **must** go." → He said I **had to** go.

Também mudam **pronomes** e **referências de tempo/lugar**: today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there, this → that.

💡 Se a informação **ainda é verdade**, o backshift é opcional: "He said he **lives** in Rio." (ainda mora)

**Perguntas relatadas** — ordem de **afirmativa**, sem do/does/did:
- sim/não → **if / whether**: "Are you ready?" → She asked **if I was** ready.
- wh- → "Where **do you live**?" → He asked **where I lived**.

**Pedidos e ordens:** **ask / tell + pessoa + (not) to + verbo**: "Please sit down." → She **asked me to sit** down. / "Don't be late!" → He **told us not to be** late.

pronunciation.tip_pt: **Said** = "séd" (não "sêid"!). **Told** = "tôuld". **Asked** = "ésk(t)" — o -ed vira um T leve e quase some: "She ask(t) me...".

reading.title: Quotes that weren't
reading.text: "Be the change you wish to see in the world," said Gandhi. Or did he? This famous quote appears on posters, mugs and social media posts, but researchers who have studied Gandhi's writings say he never wrote or said those exact words. He did write something with a similar idea, but in a much longer and more complex sentence. The same thing has happened to many other famous people. Einstein is often quoted as saying that doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results is "the definition of insanity" — but there's no evidence he ever said it. And Marie Antoinette almost certainly never told hungry French peasants to "eat cake". Why do fake quotes spread so easily? Psychologists suggest that a sentence seems more true and more wise when it's attached to a famous name. So the next time someone tells you that a celebrity said something brilliant, you might want to ask a simple question: "Where exactly did they say it?"

questions.q: Why do fake quotes spread easily, according to psychologists?

writing.model:
The conversation that changed my career

Five years ago, I was unhappy in my job and didn't know what to do. One evening, I had coffee with my former university professor, Dr. Helena Ramos. She asked me what I really enjoyed doing. When I said I didn't know, she smiled and told me that was the most honest answer I could give.

She explained that most people waited for clarity before taking action, but that clarity usually came after action. She admitted that she had changed careers three times before becoming a professor. Then she suggested that I try one small project outside my job every month.

Before we said goodbye, she warned me that the first few months would feel uncomfortable. She also reminded me that failing at a small project was the cheapest lesson I would ever get.

I followed her advice. A year later, one of those small projects became my new career in UX design. I still remember everything she told me that day.

grammar.title: Past perfect simple x continuous
grammar.explanation_pt:
Os dois olham para **antes de um ponto do passado**:

**Past perfect simple (had + particípio)** → ação **concluída** antes de outro momento passado; foco no **resultado** ou na **quantidade**:
- "By the time she was 25, she **had written** three books."
- "When I arrived, the meeting **had** already **started**."
- "He **had never seen** the sea before that trip."

**Past perfect continuous (had been + -ing)** → atividade **em andamento por um período** até um momento do passado; foco na **duração** ou na **causa** de algo:
- "She **had been working** as a nurse **for ten years** when she decided to study medicine."
- "His eyes were red because he **had been crying**."
- "They **had been trying** to have a baby for years before their daughter was born."

Mesma lógica do present perfect simple x continuous — só que **um passo para trás**.

**Conectores úteis:**
- **by the time** + past simple, ... past perfect: "By the time we arrived, they **had left**."
- **before / after / when / once / until**
- **already, just, never... before, for, since**

**Estrutura de uma biografia:** past simple para a linha principal dos fatos; past perfect para voltar no tempo e explicar o contexto; past continuous para cenas: "In 2008, she **launched** her app. She **had been developing** it for three years, and she **had been rejected** by fifteen investors. On the day of the launch, she **was** still **sleeping** on her friend's sofa."

lines.en: In 2015, Ana Ribeiro launched an app that connected small farmers directly with restaurants. Within two years, it had become one of the fastest-growing startups in Brazil. reading.title: Late bloomers
reading.text: We often celebrate young geniuses: the teenage tech founder, the 20-year-old Olympic champion. But many remarkable people achieved success much later. Before she published the first Harry Potter book at 32, J.K. Rowling had been rejected by numerous publishers and had been living as a single mother on very little money. The fashion designer Vera Wang had worked as a journalist and figure skater before she designed her first dress at 40. Colonel Sanders had tried many careers — and failed at several — before he started franchising his fried chicken in his sixties. In Brazil, the writer Cora Coralina had been writing poetry for most of her life, but her first book wasn't published until she was 75. Researchers who study creativity suggest that there are different types of creators: some make their breakthroughs early through bold experiments, while others need decades of accumulated experience. The lesson? If you haven't found your path by 30 — or 50 — you're in very good company.

writing.model:
Cora Coralina: a poet who never gave up

Ana Lins dos Guimarães Peixoto Bretas, known as Cora Coralina, was born in 1889 in the city of Goiás. She had only four years of formal education, but she had been writing poems and short stories since she was a teenager.

For most of her life, however, few people read her work. She got married, moved to the state of São Paulo and raised her children. To support her family, she sold books and, later, she made and sold sweets. All this time, she had been writing in secret.

The turning point came in 1965. By then, she had returned to her hometown, where she was living in an old house by the river. That year, her first book was finally published — she was 75 years old. Years later, the famous poet Carlos Drummond de Andrade praised her work, and she became known all over Brazil.

By the time she died in 1985, Cora Coralina had become a symbol of resilience. Her story reminds us that it's never too late to share your voice.

grammar.title: Second conditional (avançado) + I wish / If only
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Second conditional** = **If + past simple, would / could / might + verbo** → situações **hipotéticas**, imaginárias ou **diferentes da realidade atual**:
- "If I **slept** more, I**'d be** less stressed." (realidade: não durmo o suficiente)
- "If we **walked** to work, we **could save** money." (could = seria possível)
- "If she **took** a break, she **might feel** better." (might = talvez)

**First x second — a escolha depende de quão real você acha a situação:**
- "If I **get** a promotion, I**'ll** buy a car." → possível, realista
- "If I **got** a promotion, I**'d** buy a car." → menos provável, hipotético

**If I were you...** → conselho (were para todas as pessoas): "If I **were** you, I**'d** see a doctor."

**Wh- questions:** "What **would** you **do** if you **had** a month off?"

**I wish / If only + past simple** → desejo de que o **presente** fosse diferente:
- "I **wish** I **had** more free time." (mas não tenho)
- "**If only** I **didn't have** to work on Saturdays!" (If only = mais enfático)
- com habilidade: "I wish I **could** sleep better."
- com be: "I wish I **were** more relaxed."

**I wish + would** → reclamação sobre o comportamento de **outra pessoa**: "I wish my neighbor **would** stop playing loud music."

rows: If I exercised, I'd feel better.
If I had a bike, I could cycle to work.
If you meditated, you might sleep better.
If I were you, I'd take a holiday.
I wish I lived near the beach.
I wish he would stop smoking.

examples.en: If people got enough sleep, they would make better decisions at work.
examples.pt: Se as pessoas dormissem o suficiente, tomariam decisões melhores no trabalho.

examples.en: If I didn't have to commute two hours a day, I could go to the gym.
examples.pt: Se eu não precisasse gastar duas horas no trajeto, poderia ir à academia.

examples.en: I wish I could switch off after work, but I keep checking my emails.
examples.pt: Queria conseguir me desligar depois do trabalho, mas fico checando os e-mails.

grammar.tip_pt: Na fala, **I would** quase sempre vira **I'd**, e **would not** vira **wouldn't**. E nunca use would na oração com **if**: ❌ "If I would have time..." ✅ "If I **had** time..."

common_mistakes.wrong: If I would sleep more, I would feel better.
common_mistakes.right: If I slept more, I would feel better.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Na oração com if, use o past simple (não would).

common_mistakes.wrong: I wish I have more time.
common_mistakes.right: I wish I had more time.

common_mistakes.wrong: If I was you, I'd rest. (em contexto formal)
common_mistakes.right: If I were you, I'd rest.
common_mistakes.why_pt: A forma padrão é If I were.

pronunciation.tip_pt: **I'd** = "áid", **you'd** = "iúd", **she'd** = "shíd" — o D é curto, mas essencial (sem ele, a frase vira presente). **Wouldn't** = "uúdent". **I wish** = "ái uísh".

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.en: My patients often ask me: "If you could recommend just one change, what would it be?" My answer is almost always the same: sleep. If most adults slept seven to nine hours a night, we would see fewer cases of heart disease, depression and obesity. The second change would be movement. You don't need to run marathons. If you walked thirty minutes a day, you would reduce your risk of many diseases. And if people spent less time looking at screens before bed, they might fall asleep faster. Many patients tell me they wish they had more time to take care of themselves. But often, it isn't time they need — it's a few small, consistent decisions.

reading.title: The Blue Zones
reading.text: Why do people in some parts of the world live much longer than others? Journalist Dan Buettner, working with researchers and demographers, identified five regions with unusually high numbers of centenarians and called them the "Blue Zones": Okinawa (Japan), Sardinia (Italy), Nicoya (Costa Rica), Ikaria (Greece) and Loma Linda (California, USA). In these places, people don't go to the gym or follow strict diets. Instead, they share some simple habits. They move naturally throughout the day — walking, gardening, doing housework. They eat mostly plants, especially beans, and they stop eating before they feel completely full. They have a strong sense of purpose and close family and community ties. If we all lived like this, would we live to 100? Not necessarily — genes and healthcare also matter, and some researchers have questioned parts of the data. But the main message is hard to argue with: if our daily lives included more movement, better food and stronger relationships, most of us would probably be healthier and happier.

writing.task: Write an opinion essay (150–180 words): "If companies cared more about employees' well-being, they would be more successful." Do you agree? Use the second conditional and I wish.
writing.task_pt: Escreva uma redação de opinião (150–180 palavras): "Se as empresas se importassem mais com o bem-estar dos funcionários, seriam mais bem-sucedidas." Você concorda? Use o second conditional e I wish.
writing.model:
I strongly agree that companies would be more successful if they cared more about their employees' well-being.

First, if employees slept better and worked fewer extra hours, they would make fewer mistakes and have better ideas. Tired people are rarely creative. Second, if companies offered flexible hours, many workers could exercise, take their children to school and still be productive. People who feel trusted usually work harder, not less. Third, if managers paid attention to mental health, fewer employees would burn out and leave. Replacing a good employee is expensive, so investing in well-being also saves money.

Some people argue that well-being programs are just a trend and that results are what matter. However, in my experience, results and well-being are connected. In my previous job, I worked twelve hours a day, and I wish someone had told me to stop earlier — I burned out after two years.

In conclusion, if more leaders saw well-being as an investment rather than a cost, both companies and people would be healthier.

grammar.title: Linguagem de decisão + estrutura de apresentação
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Apresentar opções:** "We have **three options**. **The first one is**... **Alternatively**, we could... **Another possibility would be**..."

**2. Avaliar prós e contras** (comparativos + condicionais):
- "**The main advantage of** option A **is that** it's **cheaper than** B."
- "**The drawback is that** it would take **longer**."
- "**If we chose** option B, we**'d save** time, **but** we**'d have to** hire more people." (second conditional = hipótese)
- "**It's worth considering**..." / "**There's a trade-off between** cost **and** quality."

**3. Discutir em grupo** (concordar, discordar, sugerir — revisão do curso):
- "**I see your point, but**..." / "**That's a good idea, although**..."
- "**What if we**...?" / "**How about**...?" / "**Why don't we**...?"
- "**Could we compromise**? **What if** we tried A **for three months** and then reviewed it?"

**4. Decidir:**
- "**On balance**, I think we **should go for**..."
- "**So, have we agreed that**...?" / "**Shall we go with that?**"
- "**Let's go for** option B. **We'll** review the results in June." (will = decisão)

**5. Estrutura de uma apresentação estilo TED (5 minutos):**
1. **Gancho** (pergunta, história ou dado surpreendente): "Have you ever wondered...?"
2. **Por que importa** (o problema): "Every year, ..."
3. **Sua história ou experiência** (narrativas no passado, past perfect)
4. **Sua ideia** (present simple, passiva, relative clauses)
5. **Evidências e exemplos** (reported speech: "Researchers have found that...")
6. **Imagine se...** (second conditional: "If every company did this, ...")
7. **Chamada para ação** (imperativos, will): "Tomorrow, try..."

rows: We have three options. / Alternatively, we could...
The main advantage is that... / It's worth...
The drawback is that... / There's a trade-off between...
If we chose A, we would...
What if we tried...? / Could we compromise?
On balance, we should go for... / Shall we go with that?

examples.en: If we chose the cheaper supplier, we'd save 20%, but the quality might suffer.
examples.pt: Se escolhêssemos o fornecedor mais barato, economizaríamos 20%, mas a qualidade poderia cair.

examples.en: There's a trade-off between speed and quality, so let's weigh up the options carefully.

examples.en: On balance, I think we should go for option B. It's more expensive in the short term, but it's worth it in the long term.
examples.pt: Pesando tudo, acho que deveríamos escolher a opção B. É mais cara a curto prazo, mas vale a pena a longo prazo.

grammar.tip_pt: Pesquisas sobre decisão mostram que, para escolhas importantes, **escrever prós e contras** e **dormir sobre o assunto** (sleep on it) ajudam a evitar decisões impulsivas. E às vezes vale ouvir o **gut feeling** — mas explique-o com argumentos!

pronunciation.tip_pt: Para uma apresentação marcante: **pause** antes da ideia principal, **enfatize** números e palavras-chave, **varie o ritmo** (devagar para o importante, mais rápido para contexto) e **olhe para o público**. Grave-se e ouça: você soa convencido(a) da sua ideia?

listening.title: TED-style talk: opening
listening.context_pt: O início de uma palestra no estilo TED feita por uma aluna de inglês.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: Have you ever pretended to understand something in English just because you were too embarrassed to ask? I have. Hundreds of times. Five years ago, I was in a meeting with clients from Canada, and I nodded at everything they said. I hadn't understood half of it. Two weeks later, we delivered the wrong project. That day, I made a decision: I would never pretend again. Today, I'm going to share three simple strategies that changed the way I speak English — and the way I work. If more people used them, I'm sure we'd have fewer misunderstandings, better meetings and much more confidence. So let's start with the most important one: asking "What do you mean?"

reading.title: The paradox of choice
reading.text: In a supermarket in California, researchers once set up a table with samples of jam. On some days, the table offered 24 flavors; on other days, only 6. The large display attracted more visitors, but when only 6 flavors were offered, a much higher percentage of people actually bought a jar. This famous experiment, published in 2000, helped popularize an idea that psychologist Barry Schwartz called "the paradox of choice": having too many options can make it harder to decide and less satisfying once we have decided. When we have many alternatives, we worry that we might have chosen badly, and we imagine how much better the other options might have been. Later studies have shown that the effect doesn't always appear — it depends on how complex the options are and how much we know about them. Still, many experts suggest a practical strategy for everyday decisions: reduce your options to two or three, decide what really matters to you, and remember that "good enough" is often better than "perfect". As Schwartz has argued, people who look for the absolute best option are often less happy with their choices than people who are satisfied with a good one.

questions.q: What happened when 24 flavors were offered?
questions.answer: More people visited the table, but a lower percentage bought jam.

questions.q: What is "the paradox of choice"?
questions.answer: Too many options make it harder to decide and less satisfying afterward.

questions.q: Does the effect always appear?
questions.answer: No — it depends on how complex the options are and how much we know.

questions.q: What practical strategy do experts suggest?
questions.answer: Reduce options to two or three, decide what matters and accept "good enough".

speaking.instruction: Part 1 – Group decision (15 min): your group has R$100,000 to improve your city/school/company. Present 3 options, discuss pros and cons, reach a compromise and present the decision. Part 2 – Final TED-style talk (5 min each): use the 7-step structure.

writing.model:
The power of asking "What do you mean?"

Have you ever pretended to understand something just to avoid looking stupid? I'm sure you have. We all have.

Every day, in offices, classrooms and hospitals around the world, millions of small misunderstandings happen. Some are funny. Some are very expensive.

Five years ago, I was working at a design agency in São Paulo. One morning, a client from Canada asked us for "something clean and bold". I nodded and said I understood. I didn't. I had been studying English for years, but I was afraid to ask. Two weeks later, we presented the design. The client looked at it for a long time and then said, very politely, that it wasn't quite what he had imagined. We had to start again from zero.

That day, I made a promise to myself: I would never pretend to understand again.

Since then, I've learned that asking for clarification is not a weakness — it's a skill. Researchers who study communication have found that people who ask questions are often seen as more competent, not less. A question that takes ten seconds can save weeks of work.

So here's my idea: let's make "What do you mean?" the most normal question in any meeting. Imagine if every team did this. If managers asked their teams to check understanding, and if everyone felt safe to say "I'm not sure I follow", we would have fewer mistakes, better ideas and much more trust.

It must sound simple — and it is. But simple doesn't mean easy.

So tomorrow, try this: in your next conversation, when you're not 100% sure, stop and ask: "What exactly do you mean?" You might feel uncomfortable for a second. But I promise you, it's worth it.

Thank you.

culture_note.title: Parabéns — e próximos passos! 🎓
culture_note.text_pt: Ao concluir o B1+, você tem base para buscar o **B2 (Upper-Intermediate)**: ler artigos e livros sem adaptação, assistir a séries sem legenda em português e participar de reuniões com mais autonomia. Certificações compatíveis com o seu nível incluem **Cambridge B1 Preliminary** ou **B2 First**, **IELTS**, **TOEFL** e **Duolingo English Test** — confira nos sites oficiais as faixas de pontuação. E continue com o hábito que trouxe você até aqui: um pouco de inglês todo dia.

Tell me the story of a big achievement in your life — what had you done before it?

review.project_pt: **Projeto final do curso — "My TED Talk":** apresente (ao vivo ou gravado) sua palestra de 5 minutos no estilo TED, usando o roteiro que você escreveu. Critérios: estrutura (gancho → ação), clareza (sem jargão, com exemplos), variedade de estruturas do B1+, pronúncia e conexão com o público. Compartilhe com a turma e dê feedback aos colegas usando reported speech: "I liked when she said that...". Parabéns por chegar até aqui! 🎓🚀
